props.title: Hail Mary

sections.content: Hail Mary represents Jean-Luc Godard's radical reimagining of the virgin birth narrative in contemporary France. The film sparked intense controversy upon release, with Pope John Paul II condemning it and protesters gathering at screenings. Godard strips away traditional religious iconography, instead following a basketball-playing gas station attendant named Marie and her taxi driver boyfriend Joseph. Like his earlier works Breathless (1960) and Vivre Sa Vie (1962), Godard fragments the narrative with philosophical discussions and long takes of the female body, creating a meditation on faith, sexuality, and modern existence.

sections.content: The film sits within a broader 1980s movement of provocative religious cinema that challenged traditional doctrine. The Last Temptation of Christ (1988) imagined Jesus experiencing human desires, while Jesus of Montreal (1989) reframed the passion play in contemporary Quebec. These films share Godard's interest in colliding sacred texts with modern life, though his experimental style remains uniquely confrontational. The extended nude scenes of Marie undergoing medical examinations become Godard's way of demystifying the virgin birth while paradoxically making it more miraculous.

Godard's formal techniques in Hail Mary reflect his late period style - long takes, nature imagery, classical music contrasted with modern sounds, and philosophical voiceover. These elements would continue in later works like Nouvelle Vague (1990) and In Praise of Love (2001). The film's exploration of faith through a female protagonist connects to other art cinema treatments like Ordet (1955) and Viridiana (1961), though Godard's version is distinctly modern and politically charged. sections.content: Hail Mary sparked a wave of films examining female religious experience through a contemporary lens. Works like Agnes of God (1985) and The Rapture (1991) similarly explore women's relationship to faith, though without Godard's formal experimentation. His use of the female body as both sacred and profane influenced later filmmakers like Bruno Dumont in Hadewijch (2009) and Outside Satan (2011), who continue probing the intersection of spirituality and carnality.
